title: iran war fallout lands hardest europes most gasdependent nations 2026 03 19
author: Gavin Maguire
text:
LITTLETON, Colorado, March 19 (Reuters) - Electricity prices in Eastern Europe and Italy have climbed faster than other parts of the continent so far in 2026, suggesting that Europe's most gas-dependent economies have been among the hardest hit so far from the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
Average wholesale electricity prices in Hungary, Italy and Romania so far in 2026 ​have all climbed by at least 12% from last year's average levels, data from energy data portal electricitymaps shows.
Those price gains contrast with price declines recorded in Spain ‌and Portugal over the same period, and also exceed the gains posted in several Central and Western European nations.
A key driver of the rising electricity costs is the high dependence on natural gas for power generation in Italy and several Eastern European nations, which rank among the most gas-intensive energy systems in the continent.
Europe's benchmark natural gas price has climbed by around 65% from a month ago following the start of the Iran war, which has resulted in the closure of vital oil ​and gas shipping lanes in the Middle East.
With Qatar's main LNG export facilities closed and Iran's largest natural gas production field struck by Israeli missiles, gas supplies from the Middle East look set to ​remain stunted.
That in turn could trigger even tighter gas supplies for major import-dependent gas consumers, at least for the near term, and could further ⁠lift electricity prices.
Italy is Europe's most gas-reliant economy, according to the Energy Institute, with around 38% of total energy supplies sourced from gas.
Hungary and Romania also rank in the top five of mainland ​Europe's most gas-dependent power systems, with gas supplying around 32% and 30% respectively of total energy in those countries.
What's more, Italy, Hungary and Romania all boosted average gas-fired electricity generation so far in 2026 ​compared to the average gas generation levels in early 2025, data from energy think tank Ember shows.
Italy's gas-fired electricity production during January and February averaged around 57.4 terawatt hours (TWh) a month, compared to a monthly average of 54.5 TWh during the first quarter of 2025.
Hungary's average gas-fired electricity output was 35.6 TWh per month so far in 2026, which marked a 36% jump from around 26 TWh a month for the first quarter of 2025.
Altogether, the average ​monthly gas generation levels seen so far in 2026 in Italy, Hungary, Romania - as well as Poland and Germany - were all at or close to record highs for that period since 2019, Ember ​data shows.
In contrast to the robust gas usage trends in Italy and across much of Eastern Europe, power producers in Spain, Portugal and France have all reduced their reliance on natural gas for electricity generation in ‌recent years.
Indeed, compared ⁠to the opening months of 2022, the average gas generation levels so far in 2026 are down 50% in Portugal, down 47% in France and 44% lower in Spain, according to Ember.
To compensate for those drops in gas use, utilities in Spain and Portugal have sharply increased generation from renewables since 2022, with Spain securing around 55% and Portugal around 80% of total electricity supplies from renewables in 2025.
France secures around 70% of its electricity supplies from its fleet of nuclear reactors - Europe's largest - and around 20% from renewable energy sources.
The predominantly clean profile of those electricity sources have helped shield those ​countries from the inflationary effects of the recent ​run up in European gas prices, with ⁠electricity costs in Spain and Portugal dropping by an average of 46% so far this year compared to the same months in 2025.
In France, average electricity prices so far in 2026 are around 29% below where they averaged during the same period in 2025.
More importantly, current electricity prices in France, Spain ​and Portugal are all less than half of Italy's, where both businesses and households are grappling with painful climbs in living costs.
Authorities in Italy ​and across Eastern Europe are ⁠currently in talks with European lawmakers on how to reduce energy costs, and on how to shift the power supplies of more businesses from gas to electricity.
However, for the near term at least, currently gas-heavy energy systems look set to remain exposed to the gyrations of global gas markets, which in turn look set to keep trending higher while supplies from the Middle East stay stifled.
That means the electricity costs in the likes of ⁠Italy and Hungary ​could keep climbing, placing even more pressure on businesses, households and governments alike.
The opinions expressed here are those of ​the author, a columnist for Reuters.
